analysis.one_liner: Adds Medicare coverage for cancer screenings, diabetes testing supplies, and diabetes education.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and died without a vote when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded Medicare to cover preventive care that seniors then paid for themselves: annual mammograms for women over 49, yearly pap smears and pelvic exams for women at higher risk, colorectal cancer screening, prostate cancer screening for men over 50, blood-testing strips for people with diabetes, and outpatient training to help diabetics manage their condition. It also waived the Medicare deductible for several of these tests. It was introduced in February 1997 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it died without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially older women who would get annual mammograms without paying the deductible, people at risk of colorectal cancer, men over 50 seeking prostate screening, and Medicare beneficiaries with diabetes who would get coverage for test strips and self-management training.

how_it_helps.text: Makes all women over 49 eligible for annual screening mammography and waives the Medicare deductible for it [S2].
Adds coverage of colorectal cancer screening, including fecal occult blood tests, sigmoidoscopy, barium enema, and colonoscopy for high-risk individuals, with frequency and payment limits [S2][S3].
Adds biennial prostate cancer screening (digital rectal exam and PSA blood test) for men over 50 [S2][S3].
Adds Medicare coverage of diabetes outpatient self-management training and blood-testing strips for people with either Type I or Type II diabetes, whether or not they use insulin [S2][S3].
Caps the Medicare payment for a screening fecal occult blood test at $5 in 1998 and protects patients from extra charges by nonparticipating physicians for colorectal screening procedures [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare program (federal taxpayers) would bear the cost of the new screenings and diabetes benefits; the effective date was January 1, 1998 [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill adds new mandatory Medicare spending without an offsetting cut or tax, so it would have increased federal outlays [S3].

It sets specific payment limits (such as $5 for a fecal occult blood test) and allows the Secretary to later reduce payments if they exceed what is needed to keep tests available, which providers could see as underpayment [S3].
It gives the Secretary authority to drop coverage of some colorectal screening tests after a review, leaving some coverage decisions to future administrative judgment rather than statute [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for seniors are concrete and directly tied to early detection of breast, cervical, colorectal, and prostate cancer, plus better diabetes management, which generally saves lives and money over time. The cost is higher Medicare spending with no dedicated funding source, and the bill includes some cost controls (payment caps, frequency limits) that doctors might find too tight. On balance it is a straightforward coverage expansion whose main cost is to the federal budget.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 1997 and never moved; the Congress ended in January 1999 with no committee vote and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Graham introduced the bill in the Senate on February 12, 1997 [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one advanced the bill, so Medicare beneficiaries continued paying out of pocket for mammograms, colorectal and prostate screening, and diabetes supplies until later Congresses acted. The federal budget was spared the new spending.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seniors kept paying out of pocket

for.name: Sen. Bob Graham
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare Preventive Benefit Improvement Act of 1997 on February 12, 1997 [S1][S5].

for.name: 5 cosponsors (4 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill [S4].

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew bipartisan cosponsorship (4 Democrats and 1 Republican), but no vote ever occurred, so the chamber's partisan divide was never tested.

industries.industry: Medical providers and diagnostic facilities (radiology, laboratories, physicians)
industries.note: New Medicare coverage for mammograms, pap smears, pelvic exams, colorectal and prostate screening, and diabetes training would have brought these providers more paying patients. The bill also capped some payments, so the gain was not unlimited [S3].

industries.industry: Durable medical equipment suppliers (blood glucose test strips)
industries.note: The bill explicitly includes blood-testing strips for all people with diabetes as covered durable medical equipment, creating a new Medicare-reimbursed market [S3].
